newsitem.title: UK: UK ruling may not halt special share payouts.
newsitem.headline: UK ruling may not halt special share payouts.

text.p: The bandwagon of special dividends and share buybacks by cash-rich UK firms may continue despite a Treasury ruling that such moves will no longer receive special tax treatment, tax experts and market pundits said on Tuesday.
After a year in which banks, utilities and others have returned billions of pounds of surplus profits to shareholders, news of the Treasury statement initially sent the UK stock market sharply lower.
Reuters Holdings Plc as recently as last month confirmed plans for a complex 613 million pounds buyback schem involving involving the issue of special dividend shares.
The company today had no comment on its plans after the Treasury statement. A shareholders meeting was due to be held on Wednesday to approve the proposal.

But experts were quick to point out that companies would seek new ways of returning cash to shareholders and as there remains no formal definition of a special dividend companies would continue to seek clearance for extra payouts.
"The bandwagon may roll on," said Robert Turnbull, a tax partner at accountancy group KPMG.

Chancellor Kenneth Clarke's statement removed some of the tax advantages which had applied to pension funds, which are exempt from tax and which had been able to reclaim the 25 percent advance corporation tax paid by companies on dividends.

Clarke said pension funds could no longer claim tax credit payments -- which currently mean that a one stg net dividend is worth 1.25 pounds to a pension fund -- on buybacks or on some special dividends.
He said the new rules would apply immediately to any company repurchasing its shares or making special payouts associated with a share consolidation or a takeover.
"When it was first announced it caused a hell of a flurry," said Scott Evans, equity strategist at UBS. "But now people have had time to look at the detail."
Experts said the biggest implication of Clarke's measure was for share buybacks.

These were particularly lucrative for pension funds, which were able to treat the difference between the buyback price and the price at which the stock was originally issued as a dividend "distribution" payment on which they could reclaim the 25 percent tax.

Evans said companies had already this year bought back some 2.5 billion pounds worth of their own stock, which he had assumed would rise to between 3.5 billion pounds and four billion pounds by year-end.
Yet the level of buybacks had risen sharply during 1996 from previous years and it was a loophole Evans said he had expected to be closed.
"This has important implications for the liquidity of the London market," said Evans at UBS, "but we had already assumed that it would be ruled out by 1997."
"It will have a big impact at the company level but at the market level it actually doesn't matter a great deal."
Yet companies generating cash surplusses are unlikely to abandon the objective of returning some of that cash to shareholders in the most tax efficient way possible.

Turnbull at KPMG pointed out that an Inland Revenue rule called Section 703 already banned tax credits on what it defined as an "abnormal" dividend -- a subjective rule which he said has always been subject to debate and legal clearance.
"The courts are not always sympathetic to the revenue," Turnbull said.
And with many firms still building up cash piles on the back of strong economic growth and aggressive cost-cutting, there remains a strong incentive to channel cash back to investors.

"There is no secret a lot of companies have surplus cash," said Terry Awan, senior tax partner at Arthur Andersen. "This is a fairly significant move that means companies will have to think of other ways to create incentives for shareholders."
Another possibility is that UK firms, criticised in the past for a reluctance to invest, will redouble efforts to find the right investment opportunities.
"One result," said Awan, "is that companies may look harder at investing that money."
